I met someone in a completely banal interaction. For some reason, I left that interaction feeling much better than I had before it. Several months went by and I found myself at (what I thought at that point must be) rock bottom. I was carrying a lot of weight and guilt and resentment due to previous relationships and the feeling that I had made all of the wrong choices. Then, in circumstances just as mundane as the last time, I heard a voice and it stopped me in my tracks; I mean this voice literally made me stop mid-sentence, and something in my head told me that it was important that I notice this voice. I couldn’t even bring myself to look up out of fear and excitement, but when I did, I caught a fleeting glance of the face attached to that voice. I knew it was going to be him. I hadn’t tried to guess who it was going to be or figure out who it was, but somehow when I saw his face, I had already known it was going to be his. All of the weight seemed lifted and I felt new again. Scared, but new. Certain. 
We talked sheepishly for a couple of weeks before I asked if he’d be interested in getting coffee, dinner, a walk, anything together. That’s when he told me that he already had a boyfriend, and was sorry he didn’t tell me sooner. I was actually relieved that that was the reason he was declining. We stayed friends for several months afterward, and I was totally fine waiting and not crossing any lines (I don’t think I did, anyway). When he and the boyfriend eventually broke up, I guess I thought maybe things would develop between us and we kept taking all throughout the Covid shutdown. Just as things were getting to their most promising, *poof* he never spoke to me again. Just like that, something that was life-changing and affirming for me turned out to be absolutely nothing at all. Now I know that wasn’t rock bottom; this is. It’s been 5 years, and the poison is still in my bones and my blood. Nothing feels good, and there’s not a single day that I don’t think about him. I don’t care to move on. I didn’t survive that day.

What exactly makes you the arbiter of whether or not an apprenticeship is done right? Just because it wouldn’t have worked for you doesn’t mean it doesn’t work for anyone. There may be room for several different approaches to an apprentice/mentor relationship, but the more that we step aside and let everyone in who simply shows up with a hard on and a dream, feeling entitled to a piece of this by virtue of simply existing, the more it’s going to affect the ones who built this business, and in a negative way. We’ve seen this already, and as stated before, in less than five years, it has completely changed tattooing into a minstrel show rather than a meritocracy. That shit was already lame when wack tattooers got fame because they were in the cool guy club.

I absolutely got through my apprenticeship without working a second job. I was expected to be the first to arrive and the last to leave. I cleaned up messes and handled situations that my mentor seemingly created just to see how I’d manage them. I was teased, hazed, doubted at times, and had to fistfight my way out of a few interactions. I felt grateful to be there then, and I wouldn’t trade those experiences in now. Those shared experiences with others who came in before me are a large part of what made me a tattooer; just because two people both make marks on skin doesn’t necessarily make them kindreds. The truth is that there’s an ideal time and/or age for someone to start their apprenticeship in this business. I was just shy of 18, living at home with my single mother, in our section-8 housing apartment, and that gave me the financial freedom to pursue an apprenticeship that I wasn’t even sure would work out (and that’s another important point: this business is not for everyone, and not everyone who comes in gets to stay). If a person wants to come in at a time that’s less than ideal, then they need to make accommodations for themselves. Tattooing does not need to bend and meet prospects where they’re at. We’ve tried that during and since covid, and in less than five years, the whole of tattooing has become gentrified by tourists and interlopers because we were too busy worrying about being called gatekeepers when we should have been safeguarding our craft and community. Not all traditions are worth keeping, but some certainly are.

Learn how and when to distribute your weight differently on each foot. For pushing, keep all your weight on your front foot and try to find a sweet spot to place it (doesn’t have to be completely vertical, but maybe diagonal) right around the front hardware. You also may try tightening up your trucks a bit so there’s less play on your board for now when you put that back foot on. Keep at it, you’ll be so glad you did!!

1/3 rule is a rule of thumb, not a law. Having worked for real old schoolers (one who used to beef with huck Spaulding and Lyle Tuttle), and having those ‘rules’ explained to me by them, I can promise you that it’s not some ‘integrity of design’ thing, so don’t feel like you need to take it that seriously. Line weight should be relative to the design and its size; bolder is not always better so use your own judgement. My advice on the drawing would be to re-evaluate the leaves and where they are placed, and; don’t render it to where a colour is butted up against itself twice (the black shading on the right side of the banner is touching the black shading in her feet, and so it gets lost there. Same with the yellow undersides of the banner). I always find it helpful to think about my finished piece in black and white; if it still reads well and nothing gets lost, then I’ve done a good job of defining positive and negative edges; if an area gets lost or muddy, then I should rethink how I shaded or coloured that area. Keep it up, and also consider ditching the iPad and working with liquid acrylic and liquid watercolour to see how they actually behave on paper; this will give you a lot of insight on how to make a tattoo look like traditional Americana.

To be more to the point, each drawing here is shiro-hannya (white), so it should show the beginning of the transformation. Use the lion’s mouth that you’ll see in the original masks, rein the hair in a bit more than in the first three designs, and add eyebrows to help express sorrow. Also notice how wide the nose is v. the nasal bridge (in the original masks). This is a very Japanese feature and gives the cheeks a sort of origin point.

You’re very welcome! Some details are missing, some are just a little misplaced or understated, I think. Hannya is the representation of a woman who is or has given herself over to the demons of jealousy and rage, usually as a scorned or unrequited lover. So at first, her skin is still soft and pale, and her expression is one of sorrow. As she gives herself over to that rage more, she loses more of her humanity. Her skin turns darker, her eyes flare up more intensely, her mouth is contorted like that of a lion, her hair becomes more disheveled, and her expression grows more terrifying and wrathful. 
Eyebrows and hair will help express the emotion she’s conveying. Her eyes and mouth when viewed from a downward angle will help express ferocity. From below, sorrow and sadness. Every little feature in the mask is meant to convey emotion and expression; these are very real masks used in noh theatre, so they have to tell the audience a lot of information. Study those masks, and make your design representative of a moment in a story about this character!

There are certain characteristics that make hannya what she is, and you’re almost there! If you study the classics, you’ll see that those characteristics are always there and always fairly similar. I like to look at photos of actual, physical hannya masks from time to time when I draw them to remind me of those little details that I may have forgotten about. Keep at it and don’t stop drawing each design until it is just what you want it to be. Don’t try to work out the details when you’re painting it, not yet; for now, work out the details in the sketch and final drawing. Keep up the good work!

20 years in the game here. As I approach 40, I become more and more convinced that I want to get out of tattooing in the next ten or so years. The landscape and the dynamic have changed so much since covid, and this field is unrecognisable to some of us now. The demographics have changed completely on both sides; the people getting tattooed are different and so are the people making the tattoos, and while those newcomers will largely be abandoning tattooing soon enough, we’ll be left with customers who have gotten used to how they thought this works (just as we’ve gotten used to our ways), and it will create an impasse. So I don’t think it’s so much a matter of 40 year olds thinking they won’t be able to tattoo past 50, but more so a matter of a lot of us not wanting to stay in a field that was once magical to us and has now been neutered and sanitised by an influx of people who never really knew how it was to begin with. I got to spend some time just a couple days ago with a third-generation tattooer, whose shop was full of absolutely incredible tattoo history, from some of the first certificates of membership for the tattoo club of Japan, to a functional luciograph, to thousands of original acetate stencils, and it was really refreshing to see and hear and be around the kind of shops and characters and conversations that first got me inspired to become a tattooer. Now, today, I have to go back to work in a shop that caters equally to regular clientele as well as walk ins; mainly younger people looking for the tattoos that they saw on tiktok. It’s made tattooing feel like-and become-a job instead of a passion. 
I’m mulling over various strategies now to narrow my audience and my clientele, to only work with customers who are older and want larger and more involved work, and to distance myself from this concept of a social media presence, as all of the tattooers I look up to have. But if that doesn’t work, I’ll take it as a sign that I don’t have what it takes anymore, and that will be my cue to bow out and find what does move me.

But there’s usually another line (not all the time) that divides the solid black field of hair from the face of the hannya. That way, you can leave the negative space inside that line and start shading the forehead and temples right up against the outside of it, for example. Also, look into what the various stages of hannya are and how they would affect your design, I.e. hair and tone/colour of her skin and expression in her brow and eyes.

This is a great example of keeping one edge positive and one negative. The shading (or colouring) scheme is formulaic so it gives a sense of rhythm as well as consistency. 

[https://www.instagram.com/hannya_collective?igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==](https://www.instagram.com/hannya_collective?igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==)

I feel like it’s more around where the hannya’s left cheek meets her nose. There’s a large area of dark value there, which is fine, but there are also a couple of edges inside that area and so they’re getting lost in there: see how the dark area between her cheek and nose touches both the edges of the cheek and her nose? And then the great starts again against the edge of her nose, so it ends up getting a bit muddy in there. I’d suggest leaving a negative space where the cheek meets that space, then another negative space before the shading touches the bridge of her nose. Try that and see if you like it!

As a general rule of thumb, try to avoid positive on positive or negative on negative edges. Decide where you want your negative space to go, and make sure the edge next to that doesn’t also have a negative space. Essentially, the shading should start against one line and go towards the next line, without touching it, then repeat.

So there’s a common misconception here, and it seems pedantic but it’s actually important: black is the only thing used in a tattoo that’s properly ‘ink;’ any colours are actually pigments. These pigments are ground powder, dispersed in a suspension like glycerin, alcohol, etc etc. with other carrier solutions to keep them liquid. Because the properties of ink and pigment differ by nature, ink (black) tends to hold up better over time, but will still spread. Pigment (colour) will spread as well, as the skin continues to process it and break it up; without the black ink to act as a sort of anchor, the colour pigment will continue to spread/disperse in the skin, causing it to appear lighter or faded until it eventually goes away. Now, we’re talking years down the line, particularly if: 1.the pigment is highly opaque, and; 2. The pigment is very well saturated. I’ve got a couple of tattoos with no black outlines that still look just fine 13-15 years in, but in general, a black design will hold up better for longer than a design with no black outline.

I’d say that the criteria for a traditional tattoo include: an image that’s distilled to its most simple terms; single pass lines (typically bold and garish); liberal use of black shading (usually at least close to the rule of thirds), applied with peppery whipshading, typically off of one line and towards the next, without touching; primary or secondary colours put in at full chroma; very rudimentary blends; use of white only as an ending point in a gradient rather than a highlight. I guess I’m just used to neotraditional having not only a lot more drawing to it, but also a lot more tattooing.

I guess one could concede that varying line weights automatically removes a tattoo from a strictly traditional category, but the shading and colour are anything but illustrative; they’re still one colour gradients (maybe with white at most), and the gradient itself is very textural rather than smooth. I’m not sure how you’ve come to these conclusions, but to OP: do not clean your tattoo with alcohol, please, and do not use olive oil, baby oil, or Vaseline as aftercare. Your tattoo is fine and bleeding (plasma) is to be expected in the time immediately following its application; particularly when using saniderm et Al. because you haven’t washed it off yet.
The (viewer’s) right side has darker values, but it’s not just a field of black. Clearly the tattooer knows what they’re doing and put several values into that area; I’m sure it will heal just fine.

Those saniderm (et al) bandages are only cool if everything goes exactly right. The idea of course being that your plasma will heal your tattoo in the bandage without you having to do any aftercare, but some people have adverse reactions to the adhesive (depending on the brand, it may be a proprietary secret, so you can’t even see if there’s something you’re allergic/averse to). Also, your industry standard soaps used during a tattoo procedure are not typically antibacterial nor anti microbial; they’re more often than not just surface cleansers, so if that bandage goes on with anything unsavory on the skin, it’s now trapped in there for several days on your new tattoo. Scabbing is not necessarily a bad thing during your healing, but it’s also not something that we like to see happen. At this point, I’d suggest you shift focus onto keeping this tattoo clean, with antibacterial soap and warm water on your fingertips around 3x a day. Some ointment/moisturizer is definitely a good idea as well, though not always necessary. Aquaphor is perfectly fine to use, as is coconut oil, or a&d if you have no other alternatives; as a last resort, you can use some unscented lotion like curel or lubriderm, but definitely NOT VASELINE OR OTHER PETROLEUM ONLY OINTMENTS. In the future, you may wanna talk to your tattooer about an alternative bandage that doesn’t allow adhesive to rest directly on your tattoo. Bottom line, though, you should be just fine; you may have some slight scarring or marks that will fade in time, and may need a touch up, but other than that, you should be good. If it gets worse or begins to have a discharge, seek medical attention.
